info.name: HR SaaS — Mobile API
info.description:
Only the endpoints the three mobile apps need, grouped per app.

**Apps:** A — Residence Manager · B — Staff (Nurse / Caregiver / Housekeeper) · C — Family Portal.

**Auth:** OTP -> Bearer JWT. Run `01. Auth` -> *Request OTP* -> *Verify OTP*; the token is saved
to the environment and every other request inherits it. No session cookie, no CSRF header.

**Tenancy:** the collection sends `x-tenant-subdomain` from `{{active_tenant_subdomain}}`, which
works locally without /etc/hosts. In production the tenant comes from the host instead and the
header is ignored, so the app should point at `https://<subdomain>.<host>` and send no header.

Each request's description names the permission it needs and states which of the roles for that
app actually hold it, so an endpoint that will 403 in the field is visible before it is built.

---

### Three fixes this collection assumes are deployed

Each was verified against a running server before and after. If a request behaves like the
"before" column, the backend is older than this collection.

**1. Bearer clients no longer need a CSRF token.** `csrfProtection` used to exempt only the six
`/mobile/auth/*` paths, so every other mobile write — clock-in, daily log, MAR, incident, panic
button, device registration — came back `CSRF_INVALID`. It now skips the check for a request that
carries `Authorization: Bearer` and no session cookie, which is safe because a browser attaches
cookies to a cross-site request on its own but never an Authorization header. A request carrying
both still needs the token, so a junk Bearer header cannot be used to opt a cookie session out.

**2. Shift-working roles can see their rota and clock on.** Nurse, Caregiver and Housekeeper held
`attendance:read` and no `scheduling:read`, so `GET /shifts` and `POST /attendance/check-in|
check-out` returned 403 for all three. All three now hold `scheduling:read`, `attendance:read` and
`attendance:write`. `scheduling:write` is still withheld — it covers cancelling shifts across the
residence, so shift *bidding* stays out of reach pending a `scheduling:bid` code.

**3. The family role no longer reaches the general client and care routes.** It held
`clients:read`, `daily-logs:read` and `appointments:write`, which gate the general routes as well
as the family ones — and those have no linkage check. A family user could list every resident in
the tenant through `GET /clients` and read an unrelated resident's care log, authoring staff
member included, through `GET /daily-logs`. The role now holds `family:read`, `family:write` and
`tickets:write` only; every `/family/*` route accepts the family code on its own, so the portal is
unaffected.

Fixes 2 and 3 ship as a migration (`20260814160000_mobile_role_fixes`) because `seedTenantRbac`
only grants defaults to a role it is creating — an existing tenant would otherwise keep the old
set.


## Tenant context

Every request below except `/public/*` needs `x-tenant-subdomain: {{tenant_subdomain}}`. Each tenant is a separate database, so the API has to know which one before it can do anything — including `POST /mobile/auth/login`, where there is no token yet to carry it. Leave the header off and the request lands in the platform realm, where these routes are not mounted, and the answer is `ROUTE_NOT_FOUND` — a 404 that means "wrong realm", not "no such record".

The one exception is **`GET /public/tenant`**, and it matters: that is the call a client makes *because* it does not yet know its tenant. `resolveTenant` runs in front of every route, so a stale header there fails the very request meant to correct it. This collection's pre-request script already does the right thing: it adds the header from `active_tenant_subdomain` on every request and leaves it off `/public/*`. A real client's interceptor needs the same rule.

A staff member finds their organisation code in the invitation email, printed with their login email and temporary password.

exec: // Mobile is Bearer-only: no CSRF header, no session cookie.
// Every route here is tenant realm except /public/*, so the header is never
// cleared the way the platform collection clears it between realms. Each
// request declares it explicitly — a mobile developer reading this needs to
// see what a client must send — and this only fills in the value from the
// environment. Removing it when the environment is empty would strip a
// header the request plainly declares, which is worse than either alone.
// /public/* is the exception: it is reached before a tenant is known, so a
// stale subdomain there fails the very request meant to correct it.
// Substring, not a path match — variables are unresolved while this runs.
console.warn('403 FORBIDDEN — this role does not hold the permission named in the request description.');

item.name: 01. Auth — shared by all three apps
item.description:
OTP login, token refresh, identity. Every app starts here.

These are the only routes exempt from CSRF today, which is why they work and the rest of the writes do not.

request.description:
Which workspace an organisation code belongs to.

**Send this one without `x-tenant-subdomain`.** It is the call a client makes *because* it does not yet know its tenant, and `resolveTenant` runs in front of every route — a stale or wrong header fails the very request meant to correct it. A mobile client's interceptor should skip `/public/*`.

Exact match on the code, which is the subdomain the workspace answers on. There is deliberately no search by organisation *name*: a partial match over names would be a directory of every customer on the platform, readable by anyone. Confirming a code reveals nothing that visiting the address would not.

`status` travels so an app can say "this workspace is suspended" rather than failing the login with something misleading. 404 `TENANT_NOT_FOUND` for a code that belongs to nobody, and for anything that cannot be a code at all — a name, a whole host, an empty value.

Typical flow: ask here once, store the `subdomain`, then send it as `x-tenant-subdomain` on every request after — including `POST /mobile/auth/login`, which needs it because there is no token yet to carry the tenant.

Public: no authentication, no tenant context.

item.name: Global Search

header.description: Which workspace this request is for. Required on every tenant route — including login, where there is no token yet to carry it. Omit only on /public/*.

request.description: The dashboard's one box across clients, documents and medications. Each section answers only if the caller holds that module's permission — a housekeeper gets no residents and a working search, rather than a 403 on a box the design puts in front of everybody. Residence scope applies exactly as it does on the lists. Terms shorter than two characters return nothing rather than the first few rows of everything. Postgres, not a search cluster: each tenant has its own database of hundreds of rows, and the ACL filtering that keeps a relative out of another resident's file is a WHERE clause here rather than an index that can go stale.

`?disposition=inline` shows it in the browser. `?token=` accepts a signed link.

Responds with `application/pdf`, not the JSON envelope.

request.description:
The manager's Pending section. `status` takes a comma-separated list — the design's three sections do not map one-to-one onto single statuses, and asking for one should not be two round-trips.

`awaiting_peer` is a swap the named colleague has not answered; `decide` answers 409 on one, so the app shows it without Approve/Decline.

Requires (any of): `scheduling:read`

Residence Manager: yes

`kind` says which of the three shapes this is, so a card does not have to infer it from which ids are null:
- `trade` — both named, the two exchange shifts and nobody's hours change;
- `handover` — a colleague named, nothing offered back;
- `cover` — nobody named, the shift goes out for bids on approval.
Only `trade` has a RECEIVING side to draw.

request.description:
Hours worked against the tenant's weekly working-time limit — the OT view of the Attendance tab.

Defaults to the current Monday–Sunday week; pass `from` and `to` for any other window, and `residenceId` to narrow to one home. `meta.window` always states the window actually used.

`meta.summary` is the counters above the list and `meta.policy` is the limit they mean anything against — read both, because the limit is a tenant setting (`working_time`) and differs between customers.

Hours are net of recorded breaks, matching `workedMinutes` on each attendance row. This is a working-time figure, not a pay figure: payroll's `overtimeHours` is a separate, per-pay-period calculation and the two will not agree.

`state` is `within`, `approaching` or `exceeded`. Rows come worst-first, so page 1 holds the people a manager has to act on.

Requires (any of): `attendance:read`

Residence Manager: yes

header.description: Which workspace this request is for. Required on every tenant route — including login, where there is no token yet to carry it. Omit only on /public/*.

request.description:
What one shift tells the next.

`status` — `draft` saves without publishing. A handover is written across a shift's last twenty minutes and gets interrupted; a draft tells nobody and hands its outstanding jobs to nobody until it is submitted.

`clientUpdates` is the part that makes this not a daily log: a graded status per resident plus three blocks — health, medication, care. Care activities are a fixed vocabulary because the incoming shift scans them.

`pendingActions` takes `{ title, priority }` — normal / important / urgent — so "monitor temperature" is not level with "doctor appointment tomorrow". Each becomes a task at the matching task priority, assigned to the incoming shift's staff when `toShiftId` is named. A bare string still works and means normal.

`incidentIds` links incidents already raised during the shift rather than copying their contents — an incident has its own reference number and its own regulator-facing report, and one event with two records is one event whose records disagree.

Naming `toShiftId` is what turns "announced to the house" into "handed to the people coming on"; `announcedTo` in the response says which happened.

Requires (any of): `shift-handovers:read`

request.description:
What has been flagged in a home.

`CareFlag` was written by daily logs and handovers from the day it shipped and read by nothing — there was no endpoint, so a carer ticked "flag for attention", one notification went out, and the flag then lived only as a row nobody could reach.

`state` defaults to `open`: a triage queue showing everything ever raised is a queue nobody works. `resolved` and `all` are there for looking back.

Each flag carries `source` — the entry or handover it came off, with the resident named and an excerpt — because "medication · 2 days ago" is not something anybody can act on. Null when that record has since been deleted.

Requires (any of): `care-flags:read`

request.description:
A short-lived link to the CIR PDF that something without credentials can open — a phone handing a URL to its own PDF viewer, an `<a download>`, a link pasted into a browser.

Returns `url` (the plain route, fetched with the caller's own cookie or Bearer token, valid as long as the session is) and `signedUrl` (the same route with a credential in the query, valid for five minutes — `signedUrlExpiresAt` says until when). The signed form is bound to that one path and grants nothing beyond it; `incidents:read` and residence scope still apply when it is redeemed.

request.description:
Poll until `status` is `ready`.

A ready row carries three ways to reach the file:

- `downloadUrl` — the plain route, fetched with the caller's own cookie or Bearer token. Never expires. This is what a web client should use.
- `signedUrl` — the same route with a five-minute credential in the query, for anything that cannot send a header: a phone handing a URL to its own PDF viewer, an `<a download>`, a pasted link. `signedUrlExpiresAt` says until when.
- `fileUrl` — the raw storage address. Kept for compatibility; prefer the two above, which are built from the host the caller actually used.

Requires: `reports:read`

request.description:
The CSV an export produced.

Use this rather than taking `fileUrl` apart: the export is the resource and the file is what it resolves to, so the same rule that decides who may read the row decides who may fetch the bytes — a residence-scoped caller gets only exports they queued, and anything else is a 404.

`?disposition=inline` shows the CSV in the browser instead of saving it.

`?token=` accepts a signed link from `GET /reports/exports/:id` in place of a session cookie or Bearer header, for a viewer that cannot send one.

Answers 400 `EXPORT_NOT_READY` while the worker is still running, and 404 once the row is ready but the stored file has gone.

Responds with `text/csv`, not the JSON envelope.

request.description:
Both sides: swaps you asked for and swaps you were asked about. A caller without `scheduling:write` is narrowed to their own either way, so `mine` is what a manager uses to see only theirs.

Requires (any of): `scheduling:read`

Nurse: yes · Caregiver: yes · Housekeeper: yes

`kind` says which of the three shapes this is, so a card does not have to infer it from which ids are null:
- `trade` — both named, the two exchange shifts and nobody's hours change;
- `handover` — a colleague named, nothing offered back;
- `cover` — nobody named, the shift goes out for bids on approval.
Only `trade` has a RECEIVING side to draw.

request.description:
The staff app's landing screen, in one request.

`GET /dashboard` is the **manager's** and answers 403 to every care role, which is why this exists. Every tile is permission-aware: a figure this account may not see comes back `null` rather than being omitted or refused, so one response serves nurse, caregiver and housekeeper — render the tiles you were given and hide the nulls.

`permissions` is repeated here so the home screen can decide its navigation without a second call to `/mobile/me`. `staffId` is null when the login is attached to no staff record, which is why `shift`, `attendance` and `tiles.tasksDue` would also be empty.

No permission required — everything it returns is the caller's own or gated inside.

Requires: no permission beyond being signed in.

Nurse: yes · Caregiver: yes · Housekeeper: yes

request.description:
Start the unpaid break you are taking now.

Until this existed `breakMinutes` could only be set by a manager's correction or a typed manual entry, so the one person who knows when their break began could not record it — and worked time is net of breaks everywhere it is shown.

Acts on your own open attendance record: without `attendance:manage` the `staffId` you send is pinned to your own, so you cannot start a break on a colleague's shift.

**409** when a break is already running — two starts and one end would silently drop the first. Read `onBreak` / `breakStartedAt` off the response or `/mobile/home`.

Requires (any of): `attendance:write` or `attendance:manage`

Nurse: yes · Caregiver: yes · Housekeeper: yes

request.description:
What one shift tells the next.

`status` — `draft` saves without publishing. A handover is written across a shift's last twenty minutes and gets interrupted; a draft tells nobody and hands its outstanding jobs to nobody until it is submitted.

`clientUpdates` is the part that makes this not a daily log: a graded status per resident plus three blocks — health, medication, care. Care activities are a fixed vocabulary because the incoming shift scans them.

`pendingActions` takes `{ title, priority }` — normal / important / urgent — so "monitor temperature" is not level with "doctor appointment tomorrow". Each becomes a task at the matching task priority, assigned to the incoming shift's staff when `toShiftId` is named. A bare string still works and means normal.

`incidentIds` links incidents already raised during the shift rather than copying their contents — an incident has its own reference number and its own regulator-facing report, and one event with two records is one event whose records disagree.

Naming `toShiftId` is what turns "announced to the house" into "handed to the people coming on"; `announcedTo` in the response says which happened.

Requires (any of): `shift-handovers:read`

request.description:
Change a draft, or submit it.

`POST /daily-logs/entries` now takes `status: "draft"`, which is what the app's Save button sends; a draft is visible **only to its author** and raises no flag until submitted. This route edits it and flips it to `submitted`.

Only while it is a draft: a submitted entry is a care record and is corrected with `POST /entries/:id/amendments`, which appends a superseding entry and leaves both readable. Editing one here is a **400**, and editing somebody else's draft is a **403**.

The staff app's "In Progress" and "Submitted" tabs filter the day view with `?entryStatus=draft` / `?entryStatus=submitted`.

Requires (any of): `daily-logs:write`

Nurse: yes · Caregiver: yes

request.description:
Record that somebody with eyes on it has seen the report.

Separate from the investigation, which is the work — a high-severity incident is supposed to be picked up inside a stated window and nothing recorded that it had been.

First acknowledgement wins: two people opening the same report is normal, and a second call returns 200 without overwriting who got there first, because that is the fact the window is measured against.

`incidents:read` rather than `:write` — saying "I have seen this" does not change the report.

Requires (any of): `incidents:read`

Nurse: yes · Caregiver: yes

request.description: Training passed somewhere else — First Aid, manual handling run by a college. There is no quiz result here to trust, so what gets recorded is the card: its number, who issued it, when it was earned and a scan of it. The assignment moves to `pending_review`, not to complete: the person who did the training is not the person who confirms it. `training:read`, because every member of staff submits their own. Leave `expiresAt` out and the course's validity period works it out — three years from 29 February is 28 February, not 1 March. A completion date in the future is refused, as is an expiry before the completion.

request.description:
Open the care thread for one of your linked residents, or return the one already running.

The portal's "New Message" screen had nothing behind it: a relative could only ever reply to a thread the care team had started first, so the first move always had to come from the home.

**Get-or-create, and mostly get.** There is one `family_support` thread per resident by design — a second relative pressing the button, or the same one pressing it twice, lands in the conversation already running. `data.created` tells you which happened: **201** for a thread that was actually created, **200** for one that already existed.

You name the *resident*, not the recipients. The server puts the care team for that home in the thread; a recipient picker would need the staff directory, and `GET /conversations/contacts` is 403 for `family` on purpose — a relative must not be able to enumerate staff.

`body` is optional, so the screen can open the thread and let the person type into it. `priority` takes `general | routine | high` and drives the "Mark as Priority" switch.

A `clientId` this login is not linked to is a **404**, not a 403 — a distinct code would confirm that a resident by that id exists.

Requires (any of): `family:write` or `messaging:write`

Family: yes
